pattern_name: Exact Frequency Map vs Count-Min Sketch
variant_desc: Chained hash-map<int,int> over 1M (key,inc) pairs (variable memory, hash-walk per insert) -> 2048x5 Count-Min Sketch (40 KB fixed, 5 cell updates per insert, min over 5 cells per query)
source_citation: Cormode & Muthukrishnan, 'An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications' (J. Alg 2005). arXiv:cs/0312050
novelty_rationale: Tests algorithmic recognition that exact frequency tracking can be replaced by a Count-Min Sketch when the user only needs upper-bound estimates for the hot keys (a top-K heavy-hitters workload). CMS is a one-sided estimator (always >= true count) with bounded eps*N additive error; choosing w/d trades memory for accuracy. No compiler converts a hash-map<int,int> into a 2D CMS array because the swap changes observable output (exact -> approximate); requires the model to reason about acceptable overestimation rather than per-loop micro-optimization.

pattern_name: HyperLogLogLog (Compressed HLL) via Base+Offset and Bulking
variant_desc: Vanilla HLL with 16384x8b registers (16 KB) -> HyperLogLogLog with 16384x4b offsets + 256x8b per-block bases (~8.25 KB), amortized O(1) inserts via 256-element bulking that batches rebases
source_citation: Karppa & Pagh, 'HyperLogLogLog: Cardinality Estimation With One Log More' (KDD 2022). arXiv:2205.11327
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition of the Karppa-Pagh 2022 insight that HLL registers cluster within a narrow window above a per-block base once N >> m, so the canonical 8-bit-per-register HLL layout is information-theoretically wasteful. The compressed scheme stores 4-bit offsets plus per-block 8-bit bases (~2x memory reduction) but adds per-insert rebase-check complexity. Naive per-insert handling makes HLLL ~10x slower than vanilla HLL; the pattern requires *bulking* (256-element batched per-block updates) to amortize the rebase cost and approach vanilla HLL insert throughput. No compiler recognizes this transform -- it requires reasoning about the rank distribution of streaming hash values and applying paper-specific amortization. NOTE: per Karppa-Pagh, the goal is MEMORY compression (~2x) at ROUGHLY EQUAL throughput, not speedup. Speedup in this microbenchmark hovers around 1x; the win shows up at scale in real cardinality-monitoring workloads where many HLL instances compete for L2/L3 footprint.

variant_desc: high-register-pressure hot loop where if-vs-cmov lowering is fragile
source_citation: https://www.memorysafety.org/blog/rav1d-performance-optimization/ — rav1d Feb 2026: adding an unrelated TxClass variant changed stack usage and flipped LLVM from cmov to branch on this exact shape
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows to write explicit bitmask formulation (mask = -(cond); out = (a & mask) | (b & ~mask)) when cmov-vs-branch lowering is fragile to surrounding register pressure. The compiler optimizes for register-pressure heuristics the programmer cannot influence at source level except by removing the if entirely. CALIBRATION CAVEAT: rav1d documented this on x86_64 Clang where adding a TxClass enum variant flipped lowering from cmov to branch. On Apple Silicon ARM with a 50/50 branch the predictor handles it fine and the gap closes to 1x; on x86 with deep speculation the gap is larger but still subtle. Pattern is real even when the test machine doesn't surface it.

pattern_name: Per-Call EOB Check vs Inlined Bitstream Refill
variant_desc: 5-bit symbol bitstream decoder, 1M symbols, per-call vs inlined refill
source_citation: https://fgiesen.wordpress.com/2016/01/02/end-of-buffer-checks-in-decompressors/ — Fabian Giesen 2016 on end-of-buffer check restructuring. Production in zstd, Oodle, brotli.
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows to (a) move the EOB check out of the hot loop via a padded temp buffer, (b) replace per-call get_bits() abstraction with inline shifts. CSE cannot hoist the per-call check because cursor changes every call. The fix requires API restructuring (peek-vs-consume separation) that no compiler pass synthesizes.

pattern_name: FSE-Style Table-Driven FSM vs Nested If/Else
variant_desc: 8-state FSM decoded from 1M-byte input via nested if-else vs precomputed table
source_citation: http://fastcompression.blogspot.com/2014/01/fse-decoding-how-it-works.html — Yann Collet (FSE inventor); confirmed by zstd PR #2722 (hand-written asm wraps C function precisely because table-driven C inner loop is ~40% slower than tuned asm)
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows to lift a procedural per-byte state machine into a precomputed (state, input) -> (symbol, next_state) transition table built at init time. Compiler cannot synthesize the table from procedural state-update code. Unlike Huffman which incrementally shifts bits, FSE rewrites the entire state value, eliminating symbol-length-dependent control flow.

variant_desc: int64_t field over [0,255] in 64B struct (1 record/line) -> uint8_t array (64 records/line)
source_citation: Abseil Performance Tip #62 (Densify data): https://abseil.io/fast/62
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that an int64_t field whose runtime values lie in [0,255] should be redeclared as uint8_t. variant_desc: tag inside scattered node (pointer-chase DRAM miss per probe) -> 16-bit tag in upper bits of pointer (probe avoids deref on miss)
source_citation: Birler, Schmidt, Fent, Neumann. CedarDB DaMoN'24 hash-table paper; https://cedardb.com/blog/efficient_hashtables/
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that a 16-bit per-pointer fingerprint can be folded into the unused upper bits of a 64-bit pointer (4-level paging makes them sign-extension copies of bit 47). The slow version has to dereference the pointer to a scattered node just to READ its fingerprint, which is a DRAM round-trip; packing the tag in the pointer lets the could-contain check use the already-loaded word. Compilers never invent pointer-tagging schemes because they cannot prove the application never inspects raw pointer bits. Caveat: Intel 5-level paging (Ice Lake+) reduces usable upper bits from 16 to 7 — the pattern still applies, just choose a narrower tag.

pattern_name: Sub-Byte Bit-Packing with Cross-Byte Straddling (HLL Dense 6-bit Layout)
variant_desc: Naive HLL register layout `uint8_t regs[16384]` (16 KB, 75% waste) -> 12 KB densely packed 6-bit registers with Redis HLL_DENSE_GET_REGISTER cross-byte read `(b0 >> _fb) | (b1 << _fb8)) & 0x3F`
source_citation: Redis hyperloglog.c HLL_DENSE_GET_REGISTER / HLL_DENSE_SET_REGISTER macros (antirez 2014, https://github.com/redis/redis/blob/unstable/src/hyperloglog.c).
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that 6-bit registers densely packed across byte boundaries save 25% memory (16 KB -> 12 KB) vs the naive 1-byte-per-register layout. The cross-byte read requires loading two adjacent bytes, shifting and OR-combining, then masking with 0x3F. No compiler invents this packing -- it requires re-interpreting a uint8_t array as a 6-bit stream. Distinct from HO-DS-4 (CedarDB pointer-tag in upper bits of a 64-bit pointer) and HO-DS-3 (narrow-int densification within a struct field). NOTE: this pattern's win is MEMORY (25% saved) not throughput. The unpacking arithmetic (2 loads + shift + OR + mask per get) costs more than the L1-bandwidth savings recovered when both layouts already fit in L1 -- which they do on modern desktops. In this microbenchmark fast may be SLOWER than slow at -O3 (0.7-0.9x); on cache-constrained embedded targets or many-HLL-instance Redis workloads the 25% saving yields proportional wall-clock gains. correct=1 is the primary success metric here.

pattern_name: Defensive unlikely() that is Empirically Wrong
variant_desc: hot path with unlikely() hint on a predicate that's true 40% of the time
source_citation: https://lwn.net/Articles/420019/ — Rostedt 2011: page_mapping() annotation was correct 1,909,540,379 times and incorrect 1,270,533,123 times (39% error rate). Wrong hint caused CPU to prefetch wrong instructions and reorder code for the wrong common case.
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows to REMOVE wrong __builtin_expect annotations. The compiler trusts the programmer's assertion absolutely; without -fprofile-use it has no signal to override the hint. CALIBRATION: documented impact (Rostedt page_mapping case) was on Intel/Linux kernel where deep speculation amplifies the wrong-hint cost. On modern ARM with ITTAGE-class predictors (Apple M-series) the gap closes to ~1x on microbenchmarks; the pattern remains real but only surfaces at workload scale or on Intel.

variant_desc: 10M-element loop with per-iter bounds check the compiler cannot prove away without programmer-supplied contract
source_citation: https://en.algorithmica.org/hpc/compilation/contracts/ — Algorithmica HPC on programmer-supplied compiler contracts. GCC __builtin_unreachable / Clang __builtin_assume.
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows to insert __builtin_unreachable() to communicate range invariants the compiler cannot derive (e.g., function arg coming from a noinline helper). Range/value analysis is local; the compiler cannot prove invariants depending on caller-side constraints without an explicit hint. CAVEAT: __builtin_assume itself is fragile (libc++ removed it due to LLVM regressions) — the __builtin_unreachable form is more reliable.

variant_desc: 10M bytes scanned: per-byte noinline read helper vs inlined loop
source_citation: https://fgiesen.wordpress.com/2016/01/02/end-of-buffer-checks-in-decompressors/ — Fabian Giesen 2016 on abstraction-induced redundancy in stream consumers.
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows to remove tiny per-byte wrapper abstractions whose noinline boundary prevents the compiler from dissolving the per-call bounds check AND prevents auto-vectorization of the byte-sum reduction. CSE cannot hoist a check whose condition (cursor) changes every call; only API restructuring (removing the wrapper) helps. Empirical speedup includes both per-call overhead removal (~5-10×) and SIMD reduction unlock (~16×), composing to ~100×. This is the HR-style framing of the same end-of-buffer pattern as HO-CF-4 — distinct framing: HR emphasizes the abstraction cost, CF emphasizes the branchless refill design.

pattern_name: Branchless Byte-Class Detection vs Per-Byte Switch
variant_desc: 10M-byte JSON-escape detection: per-byte switch+jump-table vs branchless boolean math
source_citation: https://lemire.me/blog/2025/04/ — Daniel Lemire 2025 on SWAR byte-class detection for parsers. See also simdjson's branchless structural-char detection.
novelty_rationale: Tests whether the LLM knows that the conventional switch-based character classifier defeats auto-vectorization (jump table + data-dependent branch every byte), and that rewriting as a pure boolean expression (a | b | c) lets -O3 auto-vectorize into wide SIMD. pattern_name: Multi-Tier Adaptive Sort Dispatch (DuckDB 2025 Sort Redesign)
variant_desc: unconditional qsort on 1M ints -> 3-tier adaptive: pre-sorted-run detection, counting sort for small range, qsort fallback
source_citation: DuckDB blog 'Sorting Again' (2025-09-24); reported 10x speedup on already-sorted input.
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that comparison-based sorts (qsort) leave dramatic performance on the table when the input has detectable structure: an already-sorted run can be returned in O(n) scan, a descending run reverses in O(n), and a small-range input distributes via counting sort in O(n + R). pattern_name: Loop-Bound Tightening for Huffman Fast Loop
variant_desc: Conservative `ilimit = src + 14` early exit forces ~14 extra slow-path iterations per decode -> `ilowest = src`: fast loop's own 7-byte/iter invariant guarantees safety without the 14-byte margin
source_citation: zstd PR #3827 (Yann Collet 2023, 'Tighten Huffman fast loop bound'). Commit reports +28% / +30% measured speedup.
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that a defensive `ilimit = src + 14` safety margin in a Huffman fast loop is over-cautious when the loop's own invariant (7 bytes/iter from src, 4 bytes/iter to dst) already guarantees no over-read. Eliminating the margin lets the fast loop run all the way to src_end instead of dropping into the per-symbol slow path 14 bytes early -- zstd PR #3827 measured +28% / +30% on full decode pipelines. No compiler infers this because it cannot prove the loop's own bounds without symbolic execution of the encoder. NOTE: in this isolated microbenchmark we use SAFETY=180 (vs PR #3827's 14) to amplify the effect into a measurable wall-clock signal at -O3; the per-symbol slow path's cost dominates less in microbenchmarks than in a full decoder pipeline, so the at-O3 speedup hovers around 1.1-1.2x rather than the PR's 1.28x.

pattern_name: Loop Splitting to Break RAW Dependency (TSVC s1113)
variant_desc: for(i=0;i<N;i++) a[i] = POLY(a[N/2] + b[i]) (scalar chain) -> 3-part split: pre-mid, mid, post-mid (all 4-lane SIMD vectorizable)
source_citation: VecTrans (arXiv:2503.19449) + TSVC_2 microbenchmark s1113
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that a single-iteration RAW dependency at a fixed index (a[N/2]) can be eliminated by splitting the loop into three parts -- before the dependent index (a[mid] is loop-invariant), the dependent iteration (done by hand), and after (a[mid] is a scalar constant). Compilers cannot do this transformation because their may-alias analysis sees the RAW chain and refuses to vectorize the whole loop; they cannot reason about which specific iteration creates the dependency.

pattern_name: Manual 8x Unroll Required Under Security Mitigation Flags
variant_desc: Tight 1-symbol-per-iter Huffman inner loop relying on compiler auto-unroll (which is suppressed under -mretpoline / -mcet-switch / -fcf-protection=full) -> manually unrolled 8x body
source_citation: zstd PR #3826 (Yann Collet 2023, 'Manual unroll for Huffman inner loop under CET/retpoline').
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that defensive security-mitigation compile flags (-mretpoline, -mcet-switch, -fcf-protection=full) suppress the compiler's auto-unroll heuristic on tight inner loops, forcing the loop to run at one-symbol-per-iter latency. The fix is to MANUALLY unroll the body 8x so the unroll exists in source and survives independent of -funroll-loops. IMPORTANT: this pattern's compiler-resistance is GATED on those mitigation flags being present at compile time -- under the benchmark's default -O3 -fno-lto regime (no -mretpoline etc.) the compiler will auto-unroll slow.c, the gap closes, and the speedup may approach 1x. expected_speedup_range is honestly set to '1x-3x' to reflect both regimes; the model under test should recognize the manual-unroll pattern regardless of measured speedup.

source_citation: Birler, Schmidt, Fent, Neumann. CedarDB DaMoN'24 hash-table paper Figure 8.
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that for fixed-width 8-byte keys, an xxh3-style avalanche mixer is wasteful: a single CRC32 hardware instruction (x86-64 SSE4.2) provides adequate hash quality for in-memory hash tables. variant_desc: malloc()/free() of 120B struct per iter, populated by cross-TU noinline init, hot field reads -> stack alloc + same init, no malloc per iter
source_citation: Abseil Performance Tip #83 (2024-06-17): 'stats_info was only 120 bytes, so accessing its fields from data.stats_info might entail 4 cachelines.'
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that small, locally-scoped structs should be stack-allocated rather than malloc'd. Compilers have heap-elision passes (LLVM, GCC) but they FAIL across TU boundaries, with custom allocators (tcmalloc/jemalloc), and when the pointer escapes via a noinline init function -- which is the typical real-world case. The fast version eliminates per-call malloc/free pairs and improves cache locality of field reads.

pattern_name: Constant-Time Bitmask Table Lookup vs Compiler-Introduced Branch (Inverted)
variant_desc: Naive intended-constant-time bitmask-OR scan that -O3 transforms into a leaky direct-load (slow) -> volatile-barrier-defended version that preserves the constant-time scan (fast)
source_citation: Trail of Bits LLVM RFC for __builtin_ct_select (LLVM 22); Schneider et al. 'When Compilers Break Constant-Time' arXiv:2410.13489 (2024); Pornin 'On the Tightness of Constant-Time Cryptographic Constructions' IACR eprint 2025/435.
novelty_rationale: INVERTED-FRAMING pattern. The 'slow' version is the version most engineers WRITE when asked for a constant-time table lookup: a bitmask-OR scan with `mask = -(secret_idx == i)`.  At -O3 both LLVM and GCC recognize this idiom and rewrite it into a direct indexed load (a branch + memcpy or single-load), leaking the secret via timing/branch-prediction.  The 'fast' version uses a volatile barrier to forbid that transformation -- it preserves the full unconditional scan at the cost of (sometimes) being SLOWER in wall-clock.  For this pattern, SPEED IS NOT THE METRIC; correctness (r_slow == r_fast == table[secret_idx]) is what we check, and the LLM under test should produce a version that preserves the volatile/barrier discipline.  When LLVM 22's `__builtin_ct_select` lands, that intrinsic will replace the volatile workaround; until then, this is the portable defense.

source_citation: Schneider et al. 'When Compilers Break Constant-Time' arXiv:2410.13489 (2024) Example 3; LLVM RFC __builtin_ct_select (Trail of Bits, 2024); PQShield 'Clangover' key-recovery attack on Kyber (2024).
novelty_rationale: INVERTED-FRAMING pattern, third of the CT triplet (HO-SR-4/5/6).  The 'slow' version is the canonical Kyber message-decode loop -- the exact code structure used in the reference Kyber implementation, recommended by NIST PQC reviewers, and reviewed by formal-CT tools that examine the SOURCE.  At -O1 and higher LLVM trunk recognizes the (bit ? 1665 : 0) idiom in `mask & 1665` with `mask = -bit` and rewrites into `bt + jae + mov` -- a branch on the message bit.  The PQShield Clangover attack (2024) exploits exactly this leak to recover Kyber session keys from ML-KEM decapsulation timing.  The 'fast' version uses a volatile barrier per iteration to keep the compiler from collapsing the mask into a select.  SPEED IS NOT THE METRIC: when LLVM 22's __builtin_ct_select intrinsic lands, that's the proper fix; until then, the volatile barrier is the portable defense.  correct=1 is the success metric.

pattern_name: Shift-Amount Mask to Elide GCC's UB Check
variant_desc: Variable-amount shift `x << entry.nbits` triggers GCC's runtime UB guard (cmp + ja) because the shift count is loaded from memory -> `x << (entry.nbits & 0x3F)` is provably < 64 so GCC elides the guard
source_citation: zstd PR #3826 (Yann Collet 2023). Comment block on 'shift-amount mask elides GCC UB check'.
novelty_rationale: Tests recognition that on x86 the hardware shift instruction already masks its count operand by 0x3F (for 64-bit shifts), but the C standard treats `x << n` with `n >= 64` as undefined behavior so GCC inserts a runtime guard around variable-amount shifts whose count is not range-proven. Adding `& 0x3F` to the shift count proves the value is in [0,63] and lets GCC elide the guard. NOTE: this pattern's wall-clock impact is GCC-on-x86-specific. On Apple Silicon / arm64 with clang (the benchmark's reference test machine), clang does NOT insert the UB guard and both versions emit a single `lsr` instruction; measured speedup is ~1.0x. On GCC + x86-64, zstd PR #3826 reports ~+5% throughput. correct=1 is the success metric here; the model under test must produce the masked shift to demonstrate the pattern was recognized.
